# Notes
 
## EHS audit questions for data center operations:
 
Here are 10 audit questions related to environmental, health, and safety that can be added to a more comprehensive checklist for data center operations:
 
- [Are the data center’s environmental, health, and safety (EH&S) policies and procedures documented and communicated to all employees and contractors?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)1 - [Does the data center have a designated EH&S manager or coordinator who is responsible for overseeing the implementation and monitoring of the EH&S program?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)1 - [Does the data center conduct regular risk assessments to identify and mitigate potential hazards such as fire, electrical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, and physical risks?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)[2](https://pcidssguide.com/data-center-audit-checklist/)[1](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx) - [Does the data center have adequate fire detection and suppression systems, emergency lighting, exit signs, alarms, and sprinklers in place?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)[2](https://pcidssguide.com/data-center-audit-checklist/)[1](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx) - [Does the data center have proper ventilation, temperature, and humidity control systems to ensure optimal performance and prevent overheating, condensation, and corrosion of equipment?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)[2](https://pcidssguide.com/data-center-audit-checklist/)[1](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx) - [Does the data center have appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) such as gloves, goggles, masks, ear plugs, and safety shoes available for employees and contractors who work in hazardous areas or handle hazardous materials?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)[3](https://hsseworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/22-Safety-checklist.pdf)[1](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx) - [Does the data center have a comprehensive training program that covers topics such as EH&S policies and procedures, emergency response, incident reporting, hazard identification and control, safe work practices, and PPE use?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)[4](https://safetyculture.com/checklists/iso-45001/)[3](https://hsseworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/22-Safety-checklist.pdf)[1](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx) - [Does the data center have a system for recording, investigating, and analyzing EH&S incidents, accidents, near misses, and complaints?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)[4](https://safetyculture.com/checklists/iso-45001/)[3](https://hsseworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/22-Safety-checklist.pdf)[1](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx) - [Does the data center have a process for conducting internal and external audits to evaluate the effectiveness and compliance of the EH&S program?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)[5](https://www.safeopedia.com/the-proper-way-to-conduct-a-safety-audit/2/4787)[4](https://safetyculture.com/checklists/iso-45001/)[3](https://hsseworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/22-Safety-checklist.pdf) - [Does the data center have a process for reviewing and updating the EH&S program based on audit findings, feedback, changes in regulations, best practices, and lessons learned?](https://ohsonline.com/Articles/2016/04/01/Data-Center-EHS-101.aspx)[5](https://www.safeopedia.com/the-proper-way-to-conduct-a-safety-audit/2/4787)[4](https://safetyculture.com/checklists/iso-45001/)[3](https://hsseworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/22-Safety-checklist.pdf)                

I hope this helps you with your audit. 😊

Electrical contractor to make adjustments to raised floor  
Scheduled for 2 weeks  
Will then shut down and single cord the client  
Install  
Commission PDU's
 
Safety: LOTOTO, Critical bypass: VESDA (under floor)
 
Rich: any welding, grinding or cutting? Ryan - No, that will happen at the shop  
Honaker: have VESDA's under the floor, so those will be isolated in the event the work would trip them.
 
Rich: did you make sure they are okay with switching to second source  
Sean: Yes, we do. They also verify new load is good on their end before proceeding.
 
Rada: Could you add specific line items describing coordination with the client?  
Sean: Client actually initials applicable boxes for acknowledgement (they are present onsite when this occurs)
 
Joe K: new SCAF study for new equipment?  
Honaker: will do, but not doing in this install and commissioning scope
 
Joe K: will removing tile adversely affect air flow/pressure?

- Create a safe space to learn, share “Purpose, Process, and Payoff”
 
- Purpose: What is our “Event to Action” or Behavior we’re trying to change? It’s going from simply mowing and edging the lawn because we must, to mowing and edging the lawn in such a way that you have an award-winning lawn.
 
- Process: We’re going to teach you how to:  
- Conduct a pre-use inspection of your equipment  
- Pre-job walk of lawn  
- Ideal time of day to mow and how often  
- Ideal height of grass  
- How to properly clean up clipping and other debris created during job
 
- Payoff: Intrinsic motivation of pride of winning lawn of the month; External motivation of meeting Brian’s KPI.
 
- Best/worst is a simple icebreaker to implement in your small group. Ask each person to share their best and worst moments from the previous week. Installing a guardrail system on a parapet roof can be a challenging and risky task, but there are some steps you can take to ensure safety and compliance with OSHA standards. Here are some tips based on the web search results:
 
- Before you start, you should assess the roof conditions and identify the hazards, such as skylights, roof hatches, or unprotected edges. [You should also plan the layout of the guardrail system and determine the materials and tools you will need](https://www.bing.com/aclk?ld=e89f81D-6ZDV1g4Ok5lRv8aTVUCUxsHL-QMOwOI7XmzlblS5HWfNT6Jdkn33dMJe_C_k1w81eJdqa999eQznK_t7QHkcA_EoKszWi2ugjUCcpdG_9PbFio2L46RElGLUeLrBgzrrvW6jxMS1sOFl5Lt-b04uFQOyBOaY-69TqFto7p7PU5&&rlid=7e064a5a3842110af73e2f739bc7b4d3)[1](https://www.legat.com/osha-roofing-safety-guidelines-worker-safety-on-low-slope-roofs/). - You should wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), such as heavy-duty gloves, steel toe boots, non-slip soles, and a climbing helmet. [You should also use a personal fall protection system, such as a harness, a lanyard, and an anchor point, to prevent or arrest a fall](http://about:blank#)[2](https://simplifiedsafety.com/blog/how-to-install-guardrail-safely/). - You should choose a guardrail system that is suitable for your roof type and meets OSHA height and strength requirements. [For example, you can use clamps that attach to the parapet, horizontal base plates that rest on the roof surface, or toeboards that prevent tools from falling over the edge](http://about:blank#)[3](https://www.fallproof.com/blog/guardrails-for-rooftop-hatches-skylights-and-roof-edges/). - You should install the guardrail system from a safe position, such as an aerial lift or a designated area with a warning line. You should avoid working near the edge without proper fall protection. [You should also follow the manufacturer’s instructions and secure all the components properly](http://about:blank#)[2](https://simplifiedsafety.com/blog/how-to-install-guardrail-safely/)[4](https://simplifiedsafety.com/blog/how-to-stay-safe-when-installing-railing/). - You should inspect the guardrail system regularly and maintain it in good condition. You should also train your workers on how to use it safely and correctly. [You should document your installation and inspection procedures and keep records of any incidents or injuries](http://about:blank#)[1](https://www.legat.com/osha-roofing-safety-guidelines-worker-safety-on-low-slope-roofs/)[5](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/docs/2014-108/pdfs/2014-108.pdf).
       
According to the web search results, the minimum height of a wall or guardrail on a roof per OSHA depends on the type of work and the roof conditions. However, the general requirements are as follows:
 
- [For guardrail systems, the top edge height of top rails, or equivalent guardrail system members, should be](https://www.bing.com/aclk?ld=e8ACwdpf4E4aQGmutFo6KliDVUCUz7ud0QR4ujomjcMslLW7t-GAE6Kq8N3e4DvsmRgD63pdh3_YtdL_-HGtl2DMr5TF0RCqn1zkmCYJzCNA7tnWiPm8R3t9G-ZvNQB_Li33v9IliP-01DJ4zn8Q37wTy7gpe-7glN0Wvf1KmfRJv0IvIF&&rlid=0a96d7fc73c11881bf69b2d5d5bf3847) **42 inches (107 cm)**, plus or minus 3 inches (8 cm), above the walking-working surface[1](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.29). [The top edge height may exceed 45 inches (114 cm), provided the guardrail system meets all other criteria of OSHA standards](https://www.bing.com/aclk?ld=e8ACwdpf4E4aQGmutFo6KliDVUCUz7ud0QR4ujomjcMslLW7t-GAE6Kq8N3e4DvsmRgD63pdh3_YtdL_-HGtl2DMr5TF0RCqn1zkmCYJzCNA7tnWiPm8R3t9G-ZvNQB_Li33v9IliP-01DJ4zn8Q37wTy7gpe-7glN0Wvf1KmfRJv0IvIF&&rlid=0a96d7fc73c11881bf69b2d5d5bf3847)[1](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.29). - [For walls or parapets, they should be at least](https://www.bing.com/aclk?ld=e8ACwdpf4E4aQGmutFo6KliDVUCUz7ud0QR4ujomjcMslLW7t-GAE6Kq8N3e4DvsmRgD63pdh3_YtdL_-HGtl2DMr5TF0RCqn1zkmCYJzCNA7tnWiPm8R3t9G-ZvNQB_Li33v9IliP-01DJ4zn8Q37wTy7gpe-7glN0Wvf1KmfRJv0IvIF&&rlid=0a96d7fc73c11881bf69b2d5d5bf3847) **21 inches (53 cm)** high to serve as a guardrail system[1](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.29). [If the wall or parapet is lower than 21 inches, then additional fall protection measures are required, such as midrails, screens, mesh, or intermediate vertical members](https://www.bing.com/aclk?ld=e8ACwdpf4E4aQGmutFo6KliDVUCUz7ud0QR4ujomjcMslLW7t-GAE6Kq8N3e4DvsmRgD63pdh3_YtdL_-HGtl2DMr5TF0RCqn1zkmCYJzCNA7tnWiPm8R3t9G-ZvNQB_Li33v9IliP-01DJ4zn8Q37wTy7gpe-7glN0Wvf1KmfRJv0IvIF&&rlid=0a96d7fc73c11881bf69b2d5d5bf3847)[1](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.29). - [For warning line systems, they should be erected not less than](http://about:blank#) **6 feet (1.8 m)** from the roof edge for work that is both temporary and infrequent, or not less than **15 feet (4.6 m)** for other work[1](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.29).

Qualified Persons Oral Board Questionnaire   
 

5. What are the different electrical activities a qualified persons and affected worker can perform. ✅

Mainly looking for LOTO. Qualified persons can perform LOTO activities while affected workers cant.  

7. What are the three elements required to complete a Job Hazard Analysis prior to working with hazards. 

Task, hazards, controls 

9. What are the five hierarchy of controls when completing a risk assessment. ✅

Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE 

11. When is retraining required for qualified persons? ✅

Every 3 years, if the qualified person has deviated from procedures indicated noncompliance, new equipment (new hazards, policy changes, NFPA70E changes 

13. What is an electrically safe work condition (ESWC)? ✅

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established 

15. What are the two exceptions for an electrically safe work condition? 

Infeasible (equipment designed in such a way that it cannot be deenergized), supports life safety systems 

17. What is Simple (individual) Lockout Tagout. ✅

One person, one lock, one source of isolation 

19. What is Complex (group) Lockout Tagout. ✅
20. How do you determine an arc flash boundary. ✅

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

22. How do you determine Incident Energy at the working distance. ✅ 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

24. How do you determine proper PPE based on incident energy.  ✅
25. What are the four PPE categories and their Cal/cm2 rating. ✅

1 is 4cal, 2 is 8cal, 3 is 25cal, 4 is 40cal 

27. What are the two conditions to be exempt from completing Lockout Tagout? ✅
28. What is an energy isolating device. ✅

Device that removes energy from equipment such as a circuit breaker or valve (I like to ask if EPO is, which it is not since it is typically wired into controls and simply removes start sequence but not energy – also indicated in NFPA70E) 

30. What information needs to be on a Lockout Tag? ✅
31. What are the steps in a typical energy control procedure. 

Risk assessment to identify hazards, notifications sent out for hazard awareness, preparations made (PPE and tools), boundaries established, equipment shutdown, equipment isolated, equipment LOTOd, equipment LDL’s, equipment attempt to start 

33. How do you perform a verification of hazardous energy isolation. ✅
34. What are the three alerting techniques that can be used keep unqualified persons out of approach boundaries? ✅

Signs, barricades, attendants 

36. What is a normal operating condition for electrical equipment. 

Installed properly, maintained properly, use in accordance with mfg instructions, panels and doors closed/secured, no evidence of impending failure 

38. What is Two-Person Verification (3-way Communication).  ✅

Controller requests operator to perform a step, operator repeats and visually indicates step and equipment to be operated, Controller confirms, Operator performs the step

7. What are the different electrical activities a qualified persons and affected worker can perform. 

Mainly looking for LOTO. Qualified persons can perform LOTO activities while affected workers cant.    
What are the three elements required to complete a Job Hazard Analysis prior to working with hazards.   
Task, hazards, controls 

9. What are the five hierarchy of controls when completing a risk assessment. 

Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE 

11. When is retraining required for qualified persons? 

Every 3 years, if the qualified person has deviated from procedures indicated noncompliance, new equipment (new hazards, policy changes, NFPA70E changes 

13. What is an electrically safe work condition (ESWC)? 

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established 

15. What are the two exceptions for an electrically safe work condition? 

Infeasible (equipment designed in such a way that it cannot be deenergized), supports life safety systems 

17. What is Simple (individual) Lockout Tagout. 

One person, one lock, one source of isolation 

19. What is Complex (group) Lockout Tagout. 
20. How do you determine an arc flash boundary. 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

22. How do you determine Incident Energy at the working distance. 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

24. How do you determine proper PPE based on incident energy.  
25. What are the four PPE categories and their Cal/cm2 rating. 

1 is 4cal, 2 is 8cal, 3 is 25cal, 4 is 40cal 

27. What are the two conditions to be exempt from completing Lockout Tagout? 
28. What is an energy isolating device. 

Device that removes energy from equipment such as a circuit breaker or valve (I like to ask if EPO is, which it is not since it is typically wired into controls and simply removes start sequence but not energy – also indicated in NFPA70E) 

30. What information needs to be on a Lockout Tag? 
31. What are the steps in a typical energy control procedure. 

Risk assessment to identify hazards, notifications sent out for hazard awareness, preparations made (PPE and tools), boundaries established, equipment shutdown, equipment isolated, equipment LOTOd, equipment LDL’s, equipment attempt to start 

33. How do you perform a verification of hazardous energy isolation. 
34. What are the three alerting techniques that can be used keep unqualified persons out of approach boundaries? 

Signs, barricades, attendants 

36. What is a normal operating condition for electrical equipment . 

Installed properly, maintained properly, use in accordance with mfg instructions, panels and doors closed/secured, no evidence of impending failure 

38. What is Two-Person Verification (3-way Communication).  

Controller requests operator to perform a step, operator repeats and visually indicates step and equipment to be operated, Controller confirms, Operator performs the step

 5. What are the different electrical activities a qualified persons and affected worker can perform. 

Mainly looking for LOTO. Qualified persons can perform LOTO activities while affected workers cant.    
What are the three elements required to complete a Job Hazard Analysis prior to working with hazards.   
Task, hazards, controls 

7. What are the five hierarchy of controls when completing a risk assessment. 

Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE 

9. When is retraining required for qualified persons? 

Every 3 years, if the qualified person has deviated from procedures indicated noncompliance, new equipment (new hazards, policy changes, NFPA70E changes 

11. What is an electrically safe work condition (ESWC)? 

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established 

13. What are the two exceptions for an electrically safe work condition? 

Infeasible (equipment designed in such a way that it cannot be deenergized), supports life safety systems 

15. What is Simple (individual) Lockout Tagout. 

One person, one lock, one source of isolation 

17. What is Complex (group) Lockout Tagout. 
18. How do you determine an arc flash boundary. 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

20. How do you determine Incident Energy at the working distance. 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

22. How do you determine proper PPE based on incident energy.  
23. What are the four PPE categories and their Cal/cm2 rating. 

1 is 4cal, 2 is 8cal, 3 is 25cal, 4 is 40cal 

25. What are the two conditions to be exempt from completing Lockout Tagout? 
26. What is an energy isolating device. 

Device that removes energy from equipment such as a circuit breaker or valve (I like to ask if EPO is, which it is not since it is typically wired into controls and simply removes start sequence but not energy – also indicated in NFPA70E) 

28. What information needs to be on a Lockout Tag? 
29. What are the steps in a typical energy control procedure. 

Risk assessment to identify hazards, notifications sent out for hazard awareness, preparations made (PPE and tools), boundaries established, equipment shutdown, equipment isolated, equipment LOTOd, equipment LDL’s, equipment attempt to start 

31. How do you perform a verification of hazardous energy isolation. 
32. What are the three alerting techniques that can be used keep unqualified persons out of approach boundaries? 

Signs, barricades, attendants 

34. What is a normal operating condition for electrical equipment . 

Installed properly, maintained properly, use in accordance with mfg instructions, panels and doors closed/secured, no evidence of impending failure 

36. What is Two-Person Verification (3-way Communication).  

Controller requests operator to perform a step, operator repeats and visually indicates step and equipment to be operated, Controller confirms, Operator performs the step

Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE 

8. When is retraining required for qualified persons? 

Every 3 years, if the qualified person has deviated from procedures indicated noncompliance, new equipment (new hazards, policy changes, NFPA70E changes 

10. What is an electrically safe work condition (ESWC)? 

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established 

12. What are the two exceptions for an electrically safe work condition? 

Infeasible (equipment designed in such a way that it cannot be deenergized), supports life safety systems 

14. What is Simple (individual) Lockout Tagout. 

One person, one lock, one source of isolation 

16. What is Complex (group) Lockout Tagout. 
17. How do you determine an arc flash boundary. 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

19. How do you determine Incident Energy at the working distance. 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

21. How do you determine proper PPE based on incident energy.  
22. What are the four PPE categories and their Cal/cm2 rating. 

1 is 4cal, 2 is 8cal, 3 is 25cal, 4 is 40cal 

24. What are the two conditions to be exempt from completing Lockout Tagout? 
25. What is an energy isolating device. 

Device that removes energy from equipment such as a circuit breaker or valve (I like to ask if EPO is, which it is not since it is typically wired into controls and simply removes start sequence but not energy – also indicated in NFPA70E) 

27. What information needs to be on a Lockout Tag? 
28. What are the steps in a typical energy control procedure. 

Risk assessment to identify hazards, notifications sent out for hazard awareness, preparations made (PPE and tools), boundaries established, equipment shutdown, equipment isolated, equipment LOTOd, equipment LDL’s, equipment attempt to start 

30. How do you perform a verification of hazardous energy isolation. 
31. What are the three alerting techniques that can be used keep unqualified persons out of approach boundaries? 

Signs, barricades, attendants 

33. What is a normal operating condition for electrical equipment . 

Installed properly, maintained properly, use in accordance with mfg instructions, panels and doors closed/secured, no evidence of impending failure 

35. What is Two-Person Verification (3-way Communication).  

Controller requests operator to perform a step, operator repeats and visually indicates step and equipment to be operated, Controller confirms, Operator performs the step 
   
 
   
Multiple crews, departments, shifts, lockbox, etc.   
   
   
Always wear higher than incident energy indicated on sticker   
   
   
Cord and plug can be removed from power source, person maintains exclusive control over it   
   
   
Name of person that hung the lock, contact information, date   
   
   
Check instrument on known good voltage or proving unite (live), check same instrument on equipment for absence of voltage (dead), then retest instrument on known good voltage or proving unite (live)

Qualified Persons Oral Board Questionnaire   
 

6. What are the different electrical activities a qualified persons and affected worker can perform. ✅

Mainly looking for LOTO. Qualified persons can perform LOTO activities while affected workers cant.  

8. What are the three elements required to complete a Job Hazard Analysis prior to working with hazards. ✅

Task, hazards, controls 

10. What are the five hierarchy of controls when completing a risk assessment. ✅

Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE 

12. When is retraining required for qualified persons? ✅

Every 3 years, if the qualified person has deviated from procedures indicated noncompliance, new equipment (new hazards, policy changes, NFPA70E changes 

14. What is an electrically safe work condition (ESWC)? ✅

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established 

16. What are the two exceptions for an electrically safe work condition? 

Infeasible (equipment designed in such a way that it cannot be deenergized), supports life safety systems 

18. What is Simple (individual) Lockout Tagout. ✅

One person, one lock, one source of isolation 

20. What is Complex (group) Lockout Tagout. ✅
21. How do you determine an arc flash boundary. ✅

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

23. How do you determine Incident Energy at the working distance. ✅ 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

25. How do you determine proper PPE based on incident energy.  ✅
26. What are the four PPE categories and their Cal/cm2 rating. ✅

1 is 4cal, 2 is 8cal, 3 is 25cal, 4 is 40cal 

28. What are the two conditions to be exempt from completing Lockout Tagout? ✅
29. What is an energy isolating device. ✅

Device that removes energy from equipment such as a circuit breaker or valve (I like to ask if EPO is, which it is not since it is typically wired into controls and simply removes start sequence but not energy – also indicated in NFPA70E) 

31. What information needs to be on a Lockout Tag? ✅
32. What are the steps in a typical energy control procedure. 

Risk assessment to identify hazards, notifications sent out for hazard awareness, preparations made (PPE and tools), boundaries established, equipment shutdown, equipment isolated, equipment LOTOd, equipment LDL’s, equipment attempt to start 

34. How do you perform a verification of hazardous energy isolation. ✅
35. What are the three alerting techniques that can be used keep unqualified persons out of approach boundaries? ✅

Signs, barricades, attendants 

37. What is a normal operating condition for electrical equipment. 

Installed properly, maintained properly, use in accordance with mfg instructions, panels and doors closed/secured, no evidence of impending failure 

39. What is Two-Person Verification (3-way Communication).  ✅

Controller requests operator to perform a step, operator repeats and visually indicates step and equipment to be operated, Controller confirms, Operator performs the step 
    

   
Multiple crews, departments, shifts, lockbox, etc.   
   
   
Always wear higher than incident energy indicated on sticker   
   
   
Cord and plug can be removed from power source, person maintains exclusive control over it   
   
   
Name of person that hung the lock, contact information, date   
   
   
Check instrument on known good voltage or proving unite (live), check same instrument on equipment for absence of voltage (dead), then retest instrument on known good voltage or proving unite (live)

Mainly looking for LOTO. Qualified persons can perform LOTO activities while affected workers cant.

Task, hazards, controls

Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE

Every 3 years, if the qualified person has deviated from procedures indicated noncompliance, new equipment (new hazards, policy changes, NFPA70E changes 

10. What is an electrically safe work condition (ESWC)? 

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established 

12. What are the two exceptions for an electrically safe work condition? 

Infeasible (equipment designed in such a way that it cannot be deenergized), supports life safety systems 

14. What is Simple (individual) Lockout Tagout. 

One person, one lock, one source of isolation

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment

1 is 4cal, 2 is 8cal, 3 is 25cal, 4 is 40cal

Device that removes energy from equipment such as a circuit breaker or valve (I like to ask if EPO is, which it is not since it is typically wired into controls and simply removes start sequence but not energy – also indicated in NFPA70E) 

27. What information needs to be on a Lockout Tag?

Risk assessment to identify hazards, notifications sent out for hazard awareness, preparations made (PPE and tools), boundaries established, equipment shutdown, equipment isolated, equipment LOTOd, equipment LDL’s, equipment attempt to start

Signs, barricades, attendants

Installed properly, maintained properly, use in accordance with mfg instructions, panels and doors closed/secured, no evidence of impending failure

Controller requests operator to perform a step, operator repeats and visually indicates step and equipment to be operated, Controller confirms, Operator performs the step

- TOR01A-SOP-Elecctrical-UPS System Static-P1-110-Maintenance Bypass
    - Link to SOP: [TOR01A-SOP-Electrical-UPS System Static-P1-110 Maintenance Bypass](https://stackinfrastructure.sharepoint.com/:w:/r/sites/Operations/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B7ED9EB6B-825D-4FD5-9EBD-0B8469C89446%7D&file=TOR01A-SOP-Electrical-UPS%20System%20Static-P1-110%20Maintenance%20Bypass.docx&action=default&mobileredirect=true)
        - Section 2 - Supporting Documentation
            - Add "STACK AMER-AP-Safety-High Risk Activities-Lockout Tagout Policy
            - Add "TOR01A LOTO Procedure"
   

A Kirk key cannot be used as an isolation device per NFPA 70E because it does not meet the requirements for ensuring an electrically safe work condition. Here are the main reasons:
 
1. **Verification of Absence of Voltage**: NFPA 70E requires the use of an adequately rated portable test instrument to verify the absence of voltage before any work can be performed on electrical equipment1. A Kirk key interlock system does not provide this verification.
2. **Physical Disconnection**: NFPA 70E mandates that an isolation device must physically disconnect the electrical equipment from all energy sources1. A Kirk key interlock system controls access and operation but does not physically disconnect the equipment.
3. **Lockout/Tagout Compliance**: The standard specifies that lockout/tagout procedures must be followed to ensure that equipment cannot be re-energized while maintenance is being performed1. A Kirk key system alone does not fulfill these lockout/tagout requirements.

5. What are the different electrical activities a qualified persons and affected worker can perform. 

Mainly looking for LOTO. Qualified persons can perform LOTO activities while affected workers cant.    
What are the three elements required to complete a Job Hazard Analysis prior to working with hazards.   
Task, hazards, controls 

7. What are the five hierarchy of controls when completing a risk assessment. 

Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE 

9. When is retraining required for qualified persons? 

Every 3 years, if the qualified person has deviated from procedures indicated noncompliance, new equipment (new hazards, policy changes, NFPA70E changes 

11. What is an electrically safe work condition (ESWC)? 

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established 

13. What are the two exceptions for an electrically safe work condition? 

Infeasible (equipment designed in such a way that it cannot be deenergized), supports life safety systems 

15. What is Simple (individual) Lockout Tagout.

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment

Risk assessment to identify hazards, notifications sent out for hazard awareness, preparations made (PPE and tools), boundaries established, equipment shutdown, equipment isolated, equipment LOTOd, equipment LDL’s, equipment attempt to start

Signs, barricades, attendants

Installed properly, maintained properly, use in accordance with mfg instructions, panels and doors closed/secured, no evidence of impending failure

Controller requests operator to perform a step, operator repeats and visually indicates step and equipment to be operated, Controller confirms, Operator performs the step

1. What are the different electrical activities a qualified persons and affected worker can perform. 

Mainly looking for LOTO. Qualified persons can perform LOTO activities while affected workers cant.    
What are the three elements required to complete a Job Hazard Analysis prior to working with hazards.   
Task, hazards, controls 

3. What are the five hierarchy of controls when completing a risk assessment. 

Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE 

5. When is retraining required for qualified persons? 

Every 3 years, if the qualified person has deviated from procedures indicated noncompliance, new equipment (new hazards, policy changes, NFPA70E changes 

7. What is an electrically safe work condition (ESWC)? 

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established 

9. What are the two exceptions for an electrically safe work condition? 

Infeasible (equipment designed in such a way that it cannot be deenergized), supports life safety systems 

11. What is Simple (individual) Lockout Tagout. 

One person, one lock, one source of isolation 

13. What is Complex (group) Lockout Tagout. 
14. How do you determine an arc flash boundary. 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

16. How do you determine Incident Energy at the working distance. 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

18. How do you determine proper PPE based on incident energy.  
19. What are the four PPE categories and their Cal/cm2 rating. 

1 is 4cal, 2 is 8cal, 3 is 25cal, 4 is 40cal 

21. What are the two conditions to be exempt from completing Lockout Tagout? 
22. What is an energy isolating device. 

Device that removes energy from equipment such as a circuit breaker or valve (I like to ask if EPO is, which it is not since it is typically wired into controls and simply removes start sequence but not energy – also indicated in NFPA70E) 

24. What information needs to be on a Lockout Tag? 
25. What are the steps in a typical energy control procedure. 

Risk assessment to identify hazards, notifications sent out for hazard awareness, preparations made (PPE and tools), boundaries established, equipment shutdown, equipment isolated, equipment LOTOd, equipment LDL’s, equipment attempt to start 

27. How do you perform a verification of hazardous energy isolation. 
28. What are the three alerting techniques that can be used keep unqualified persons out of approach boundaries? 

Signs, barricades, attendants 

30. What is a normal operating condition for electrical equipment . 

Installed properly, maintained properly, use in accordance with mfg instructions, panels and doors closed/secured, no evidence of impending failure 

32. What is Two-Person Verification (3-way Communication).  

Controller requests operator to perform a step, operator repeats and visually indicates step and equipment to be operated, Controller confirms, Operator performs the step

Task, hazards, controls

Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE 

5. When is retraining required for qualified persons? 

Every 3 years, if the qualified person has deviated from procedures indicated noncompliance, new equipment (new hazards, policy changes, NFPA70E changes 

7. What is an electrically safe work condition (ESWC)? 

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established 

9. What are the two exceptions for an electrically safe work condition? 

Infeasible (equipment designed in such a way that it cannot be deenergized), supports life safety systems 

11. What is Simple (individual) Lockout Tagout. 

One person, one lock, one source of isolation 

13. What is Complex (group) Lockout Tagout.

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

16. How do you determine Incident Energy at the working distance. 

Arc flash assessment, sticker on equipment 

18. How do you determine proper PPE based on incident energy.  
19. What are the four PPE categories and their Cal/cm2 rating. 

1 is 4cal, 2 is 8cal, 3 is 25cal, 4 is 40cal 

21. What are the two conditions to be exempt from completing Lockout Tagout? 
22. What is an energy isolating device. 

Device that removes energy from equipment such as a circuit breaker or valve (I like to ask if EPO is, which it is not since it is typically wired into controls and simply removes start sequence but not energy – also indicated in NFPA70E) 

24. What information needs to be on a Lockout Tag? 
25. What are the steps in a typical energy control procedure. 

Risk assessment to identify hazards, notifications sent out for hazard awareness, preparations made (PPE and tools), boundaries established, equipment shutdown, equipment isolated, equipment LOTOd, equipment LDL’s, equipment attempt to start 

27. How do you perform a verification of hazardous energy isolation. 
28. What are the three alerting techniques that can be used keep unqualified persons out of approach boundaries? 

Signs, barricades, attendants 

30. What is a normal operating condition for electrical equipment . 

Installed properly, maintained properly, use in accordance with mfg instructions, panels and doors closed/secured, no evidence of impending failure 

32. What is Two-Person Verification (3-way Communication).  

Controller requests operator to perform a step, operator repeats and visually indicates step and equipment to be operated, Controller confirms, Operator performs the step

The equipment has be isolated, deenergized, LOTO’d, LDL’s, tested, boundaries established

**Environmental Health & Safety:**

1. **Audits & Inspections Conducted:** Proactive, third-party or in-house audits, not including regulatory inspections or audits conducted. These include those of significance performed no more frequently than monthly. This does not include HRA assessments, or risk specific audits. The intention is to capture more comprehensive audits conducted on a monthly, quarterly or annual basis.
2. **% of Compliance Findings Closed:** A percentage of compliance findings closed from all audits reported on.
3. **% of Employees Submitting EHS Observations:**  A percentage of STACK employees that have submitted observations during the reporting period. 
    - **Data source:** SOSPES
4. **% of Positive Observations and Suggestions​:** The percentage of positive observations or actionable suggestions for safety improvements reported during the reporting period.
    - **Data source:** SOSPES
5. **% of EHS Trainings Completed:** The percentage of EHS trainings completed by employees.
    - **Data source:** Learning Management System (LMS)

Audit dashboard issue update

- Donna reached out to me last Wednesday when she was reviewing the dashboard and she thought the number of "recommendations" for CHI01A was too many and looked out of place
- In looking at the "source of truth" spreadsheet for CHI01A, we noticed that what was being reflected on the dashboard were the total number of recommendations, regardless of whether or not they were tied to N/A, Met, Partially Met, or Not Met
- Recommendations associated with audit criteria/line items that were N/A or Met were still showing on the dashboard and could be misinterpreted as audit findings.
- Short term work around - each EHS Manager should make sure their respective "source of truth" spreadsheets do not have verbiage in the recommendations field if they are not actually findings from the audit. If this situation is found, cut/copy/paste the recommendation into the "notes" field. Doing so will more accurately reflect how many findings there were and how many of those findings are still open or have been closed.
- Long term fix - adjust Dashboard code to pull actual findings (partially or not met items) vs. pulling total number of recommendations.

7. Verify that the condition or event has been fully investigated and documented. 
8. Verify that corrective actions have been implemented and are effective. 
9. Verify that any necessary preventive actions have been identified and are being taken. 
10. Review any procedural or training changes that have been made to prevent a recurrence. 
11. Verify that any regulatory requirements or commitments have been met. 
12. Review any notifications that have been made to regulatory agencies or other stakeholders. 
13. Verify that all affected personnel have been informed of the condition or event and its resolution. 
14. Verify that the SOSPES report has been properly classified in accordance with applicable criteria. 
    1. Call local team who completed SOSPES report for clarification and acknowledgement. 
    2. If SOSPES observations should be a SiD make sure to update the label in SOSPES for proper routing.

15. If immediate corrective actions are completed and all sections have been completed correctly add a note and close report.

Here's a gap analysis between the "STACK AMER-AP-Safety-Business Continuity Plans-Site-Specific Emergency Response Plan" and the "Disaster Recovery and Continuity Plan_Current Doc_DN to review and sunset with the ERP Update".
 
**1. Purpose and Scope:**
 
- **Emergency Response Plan (ERP):** Ensures adequate emergency preparedness with rapid and appropriate response to emergency situations such as life-threatening injuries, natural disasters, chemical spills, fires, explosions, and other hazards.  
- **Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP):** Focuses on the quick and effective recovery of critical business functions following any event that causes the loss or limited use of facilities and services, ensuring compliance with U.S. OSHA regulations.
 
**2. Key Responsibilities:**
 
- **ERP:** Specifies roles for the Critical Operations Manager, Site Security, Environmental, Health, and Safety (EHS) team, and all employees during emergency situations.  
- **DRP:** Includes responsibilities for Crisis Management Team, Security, Operations & Engineering, Customer Relations, and Housekeeping during disaster recovery phases.
 
**3. Procedures:**
 
- **ERP:** Details specific procedures for various emergencies such as medical, fire, diesel fuel spill, chemical spill, active shooter, earthquake, severe weather, and other emergencies.  
- **DRP:** Outlines response procedures for specific disaster types including natural disasters, fire, chemical emergencies, civil disturbances, and security threats. Also includes business continuity and recovery steps.
 
**4. Training and Drills:**
 
- **ERP:** Requires training for all employees on emergency response plans, including initial and annual training sessions.  
- **DRP:** Emphasizes training for emergency preparedness and business continuity, including periodic drills and exercises.
 
**5. Communication Protocols:**
 
- **ERP:** Includes communication protocols for emergencies, specifying tools like email, instant messaging, cellular phones, and radios.  
- **DRP:** Details communication equipment and procedures for emergency notifications and coordination during response and recovery.
 
**6. Resource and Equipment Requirements:**
 
- **ERP:** Lists emergency resources and equipment such as first aid kits, AEDs, fire extinguishers, radios, emergency water, and evacuation supplies.  
- **DRP:** Specifies equipment for emergency response and business continuity, including maintenance and inspection protocols.
 
**7. Documentation and Review:**
 
- **ERP:** Requires documentation of emergency drills and maintenance of related procedures in the NetSuite system.  
- **DRP:** Includes sections for documentation, review, and updates to ensure the plan remains current and effective.
 
In summary, the ERP focuses more on immediate response to emergencies, while the DRP covers both immediate response and long-term recovery and business continuity. Both plans have overlapping elements but cater to different phases of managing emergencies.

It sounds like the reorganization of your SharePoint library has broken the links to your source spreadsheets in Power BI. Here’s how you can re-link them:

1. **Open Power BI Desktop**: Start by opening your Power BI Desktop application.
2. **Edit Queries**:
    - Go to the **Home** tab.
    - Click on **Transform data** to open the Power Query Editor.
3. **Locate Broken Links**:
    - In the Power Query Editor, look for any queries that are showing errors. These are likely the ones with broken links.
4. **Update Data Source Settings**:
    - Select the query with the broken link.
    - In the **Query Settings** pane, click on the **Source** step.
    - Update the file path to the new location of your spreadsheet in the reorganized SharePoint library.
5. **Re-authenticate if Necessary**:
    - If prompted, re-enter your credentials to access the SharePoint library.
6. **Apply Changes**:
    - After updating all necessary links, click **Close & Apply** to save your changes and refresh the data.
7. **Verify Data Refresh**:
    - Ensure that the data refreshes correctly and that your dashboard reflects the latest changes.

If you have multiple spreadsheets, you might need to repeat these steps for each one. Let me know if you need more detailed guidance on any of these steps! 😊

In Power BI, the different colors used in code or DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) help to distinguish various elements and improve readability. Here’s a breakdown of what the colors typically represent:

1. **Keywords**: Keywords like IF, SWITCH, SUM, and SELECTEDVALUE are usually highlighted in **blue**. This helps to quickly identify the core functions and commands in your DAX formulas.
2. **Variables**: Variables declared using the VAR keyword are often shown in **green**. This makes it easier to spot where variables are defined and used within your code.
3. **Strings**: Text strings enclosed in double quotes are typically displayed in **red**. This helps to differentiate between text and other types of data.
4. **Numbers**: Numeric values are usually shown in **black** or **dark blue**, making them stand out from text and keywords.
5. **Comments**: Comments added to your code using // for single-line comments or /* ... */ for multi-line comments are often displayed in **gray**. This helps to separate explanatory notes from the executable code.
6. **Functions and Measures**: Custom functions and measures you create are usually highlighted in **purple**. This helps to distinguish them from built-in functions and keywords.

These color conventions can vary slightly depending on the theme or settings you use in Power BI, but they generally follow these patterns to enhance code readability and debugging.

Enjoy!  -Spencer   **What happens to cause an arc flash in an A/C system?** In an AC (alternating current) system, an arc flash occurs due to the breakdown of insulation or air that normally separates energized conductors or between a conductor and ground. Here’s what happens to the AC current that can lead to an arc flash:   1. Current Path Disruption In AC systems, the voltage and current alternate direction periodically. Under normal circumstances, this current flows through conductors, which are insulated to prevent contact with air, other conductors, or ground. If the insulation or air gap between conductors breaks down, an unintended path for the current is created. This allows current to “jump” across the gap through the air, forming an arc.   2. Ionization of Air An arc flash typically occurs when the electric field (voltage difference) becomes strong enough to ionize the air between two conductive points. Ionization happens when air particles (atoms or molecules) gain or lose electrons, turning the air into a conductive plasma. Once the air becomes ionized, it provides a low-resistance path for the AC current to flow, causing an arc.   AC current alternates direction: Even though the current reverses direction, the high voltage and ionized air allow the arc to sustain itself across the air gap. 3. Energy Release As the current flows through the ionized air (arc plasma), the energy is rapidly released in the form of:   Intense heat: Arc temperatures can reach upwards of 35,000°F (about 19,400°C), which is hotter than the surface of the sun. This heat can melt metal components and cause severe burns. Light: A bright flash of light is emitted, which can cause eye damage (arc eye) if protection is not used. Pressure wave: The intense heat and energy can create an explosive pressure wave that throws molten metal and debris outward. Sound blast: The arc flash often produces a loud noise that can damage hearing. 4. Sustaining the Arc Even though the AC current alternates between positive and negative cycles, the arc can continue because:   Air remains ionized: Once the air is ionized, it remains conductive even as the AC current changes direction. Equipment damage and degradation: As the arc melts metal conductors or equipment, the gap between conductors may widen or change, but as long as there’s sufficient voltage to ionize the air, the arc can persist.   **What’s happening to electrons in an arc flash?** In an arc flash, electrons undergo several critical processes as the electrical energy is discharged:   Ionization of air or other medium: Normally, air acts as an insulator between conductors. However, when the voltage across a gap becomes high enough, it can break down the insulating properties of the air. The high electric field causes electrons in the air molecules to be stripped away (ionization), creating a plasma—a highly conductive mixture of ions and free electrons.   Current flow through plasma: Once the air is ionized and becomes plasma, the free electrons can move more easily between atoms. The arc provides a low-resistance path for current, allowing a large number of electrons to flow through the plasma. These electrons carry electrical current, and their movement is responsible for the transfer of energy that sustains the arc.   Acceleration of electrons: Electrons in the arc are accelerated by the strong electric field between the conductors. As they accelerate, they collide with gas atoms or molecules (such as air), causing excitation and ionization. These collisions release large amounts of energy in the form of heat, light, and electromagnetic radiation.   Energy release from electron collisions: As electrons collide with atoms in the arc, they knock other electrons off atoms (further ionizing the air), and in the process, they release energy. This energy is what creates the intense heat, light, and sound of the arc flash. The electrons themselves lose energy during these collisions, but the electric field quickly re-accelerates them, maintaining the arc.   Recombination of electrons and ions: Eventually, after the arc is extinguished, electrons will recombine with ions in the surrounding air. During this process, energy in the form of heat and light is released. This contributes to the bright flash and extreme temperatures seen in an arc flash event.   Overall, during an arc flash, electrons are rapidly stripped from atoms, accelerated through a plasma, and constantly colliding and releasing energy, which creates the destructive energy output of the arc.         | | |---| |\| \| \|

2. Hover your cursor over this guy and click
3. It will open up the "card"
4. You can see all the other "properties" in this view also
5. Consider adding your daily notes as follows
    1. Go to lower half of the card
    2. Hit forward slash "/"
    3. Type "collapsable heading" (1, 2, or 3)
    4. Type "Notes"
    5. Hit enter
    6. Type forward slash "/"
    7. Type "date"
    8. Choose the applicable day from the calendar that populates
    9. Once the date is chosen, you can then type any/all the notes you'd like to add for that particular day for that particular task (or sub-tasks)

## Question #1: _"What is the difference between fall protection versus fall restraint?"_
 
The primary difference between **fall protection** and **fall restraint** lies in their purpose and how they are designed to manage the risk of falling:  
**1. Fall Protection**

- **Purpose**: Protects a worker after they have fallen by stopping or arresting the fall to prevent serious injury.
- **Key Features**:
    - Involves systems like **personal fall arrest systems**, which include a **harness**, **lanyard**, and **anchor point**.
    - Allows the worker to access areas where a fall is possible but ensures the fall is stopped within a safe distance (no more than 6 feet of free fall is typically allowed).
    - **Examples**:
        - Using a full-body harness and shock-absorbing lanyard on a mobile elevated platform.
        - Anchoring to a lifeline when working on a roof without guardrails.
    - Requires additional safety planning for **rescue procedures** in case the worker becomes suspended.
 
**2. Fall Restraint**

- **Purpose**: Prevents a worker from reaching a fall hazard, effectively eliminating the risk of falling altogether.
- **Key Features**:
    - Uses a system to physically restrain or limit the worker's movement so they cannot get close to the fall hazard.
    - Usually involves a **harness** or **body belt**, a **restraint lanyard**, and an **anchor point**.
    - **Examples**:
        - A worker on a roof uses a short lanyard that prevents them from getting close to the roof edge.
        - A worker on a platform is tethered to an anchor point that limits their range of movement.
    - Does not require a rescue plan since the worker cannot fall.
 
**Key Differences:**

|   |   |   |
|---|---|---|
|**Aspect**|**Fall Protection**|**Fall Restraint**|
|**Purpose**|Protects after a fall has occurred.|Prevents the worker from reaching the hazard.|
|**Use Case**|Where falls are possible but must be arrested.|Where falls can be completely prevented.|
|**System Components**|Full-body harness, shock-absorbing lanyard, self-retracting lifeline (SRL), anchor points.|Body belt or harness, fixed-length lanyard, anchor points.|
|**Rescue Plan**|Required (for suspension after fall arrest).|Not required.|
 
**When to Use Which?**

- **Fall Restraint**: Preferred when possible because it eliminates the fall risk entirely. For example, working near a roof edge with a lanyard that keeps the worker away from the edge.
- **Fall Protection**: Used when fall restraint isn’t feasible or practical, such as working on a scaffold or an aerial lift where a fall arrest system is needed to stop a potential fall.

## Question #2: _"If I have a contractor working on a mobile elevated platform, do they have to wear fall protection?"_
 
Yes, contractors working on a mobile elevated platform (MEWP) **must wear fall protection** as per the STACK AMER Mobile Elevated Platform Procedure and OSHA regulations. Here are the key requirements:  
**Fall Protection for MEWPs**

1. **Full Body Harness**:
    - Contractors must wear a full body harness.
    - The harness must be attached to the manufacturer’s engineered anchor point on the MEWP basket or platform.
2. **Restraint System Lanyard**:
    - A restraint system lanyard should be used to prevent the individual from being ejected from the platform or falling over the guardrails.
3. **Prohibited Practices**:
    - Standing on handrails, mid-rails, or top rails is strictly prohibited.
    - Self-retracting lanyards are not permitted for use in MEWPs unless specifically allowed by the manufacturer.
4. **Job Safety Analysis (JSA)**:
    - Fall protection requirements, including proper harness use, must be documented in the Job Safety Analysis (JSA) for the work activity.
5. **Training Requirements**:
    - Contractors must have completed appropriate training on fall protection systems as outlined in the Mobile Elevated Platform Procedure and Fall Protection Procedure【11†source】【15†source】.

**Additional MEWP Safety Considerations**

- Ensure a spotter is present when the MEWP is in motion or near hazards.
- Barricade the area below the MEWP to protect others from falling objects.
- Inspect the MEWP and all fall protection equipment before use.

Following these guidelines ensures compliance with STACK AMER safety policies and OSHA regulations while safeguarding contractors' safety. If you have specific questions about the task or equipment, let me know!

## Question #3: _"Do I have to fill out a confined space permit if I have contractors entering an electrical vault?"_
 
Yes, you need to fill out a confined space permit if contractors are entering an electrical vault that qualifies as a **permit-required confined space**. Electrical vaults often fall into this category due to the following reasons:

1. **Hazardous Atmosphere**: Electrical vaults may accumulate gases like hydrogen from batteries or other harmful vapors, which could lead to oxygen deficiency or create a flammable atmosphere.
2. **Electrical Hazards**: The presence of live electrical equipment poses a significant risk, making it necessary to isolate the energy source (using Lockout/Tagout procedures) and ensure proper safety measures are in place.
3. **Configuration Hazards**: Vaults may have limited access points or other structural features that increase risks to entrants.
4. **Other Hazards**: Potentially high temperatures, poor ventilation, or other safety hazards.

**Steps to Take:**

1. **Evaluate the Vault**: Conduct a confined space hazard assessment using your facility's **Confined Space Assessment Form** to determine if it is a permit-required confined space.
2. **Fill Out the Permit**: If the vault is deemed permit-required, prepare a confined space permit, ensuring all hazards are documented, proper controls are in place, and the necessary atmospheric testing is completed before entry【10†source】.
3. **Coordinate with Contractors**:
    - Provide them with a copy of your facility's confined space policy.
    - Ensure contractors are trained and understand their roles and responsibilities under your confined space entry procedures.
    - Confirm the contractors’ procedures meet or exceed your internal safety requirements.

Remember to also verify that **emergency rescue resources** are on-site or readily available and that communication between the contractors, attendants, and supervisors is established. If you’re uncertain about specific hazards or procedures, consult your safety or operations manager.

## Question #4: _"When do I need to execute a confined space permit?"_
 
A confined space permit is required whenever a permit-required confined space is identified and entry is necessary. Permit-required confined spaces are spaces that meet the following conditions:

1. **Hazardous Atmosphere**: The space contains or has the potential to contain a hazardous atmosphere, such as oxygen deficiency, flammable gases, or toxic substances.
2. **Engulfment Hazards**: The space contains materials that could potentially engulf an entrant.
3. **Configuration Hazards**: The internal configuration could trap or asphyxiate an entrant due to inwardly converging walls or a floor that slopes downward and tapers to a smaller cross-section.
4. **Other Recognized Hazards**: The space contains any other serious safety or health hazard.

The confined space permit ensures:

- Pre-entry atmospheric testing is conducted.
- All hazards are identified, and control measures are in place.
- Entry supervisors authorize the entry, and attendants and authorized entrants are assigned.
- Emergency rescue plans and resources are available【10†source】.

==Also, the “employer can demonstrate that installation of a ground is impracticable” language below. When I was with a utility, that sentence is difficult to defend so we defaulted to installation of personal protective grounds for all work.==  
   
==Anyway, interested in hearing your opinion on below.==  
   
==Also, see here for the “Basics of Personal Protective Grounding”==  
==The Basics of Personal Protective Grounding | EC&M==  
   
==Thanks!==  
   
   
**1910.269 - Electric power generation, transmission, and distribution**  
   
==1910.269 - Electric power generation, transmission, and distribution. | Occupational Safety and Health Administration==  
   
==1910.269(a)(1)(i)(A)==  
==Power generation, transmission, and distribution installations, including related equipment for the purpose of communication or metering that are accessible only to qualified employees;==  
==NOTE TO PARAGRAPH (a)(1)(i)(A): The types of installations covered by this paragraph include the generation, transmission, and distribution installations of electric utilities,== ==as well as equivalent installations of industrial establishments.== ==Subpart S of this part covers supplementary electric generating equipment that is used to supply a workplace for emergency, standby, or similar purposes only. (See paragraph (a)(1)(i)(B) of this section.)==  
   
==1910.269(m)==  
**Deenergizing lines and equipment for employee protection** ==-==  
   
==1910.269(m)(3)==  
**Deenergizing lines and equipment**==.==  
   
==1910.269(m)(3)(vii)==  
==The employer shall ensure the installation of protective grounds as required by paragraph (n) of this section.==  
   
==1910.269(n)==  
**Grounding for the protection of employees** ==-==  
==1910.269(n)(1)==  
**Application**==. Paragraph (n) of this section applies to grounding of generation, transmission, and distribution lines and equipment for the purpose of protecting employees. Paragraph (n)(4) of this section also applies to protective grounding of other equipment as required elsewhere in this section.==  
==Note to paragraph (n)(1): This paragraph covers grounding of generation, transmission, and distribution lines and equipment when this section requires protective grounding and whenever the employer chooses to ground such lines and equipment for the protection of employees.==  
==1910.269(n)(2)==  
**General**==. For any employee to work transmission and distribution lines or equipment as deenergized, the employer shall ensure that the lines or equipment are deenergized under the provisions of paragraph (m) of this section and shall ensure proper grounding of the lines or equipment as specified in paragraphs (n)(3) through (n)(8) of this section.== ==However, if the employer can demonstrate that installation of a ground is impracticable or that the conditions resulting from the installation of a ground would present greater hazards to employees than working without grounds, the lines and equipment may be treated as deenergized provided that the employer establishes that all of the following conditions apply:==  
==1910.269(n)(2)(i)==  
==The employer ensures that the lines and equipment are deenergized under the provisions of paragraph (m) of this section.==  
==1910.269(n)(2)(ii)==  
==There is no possibility of contact with another energized source.==

_OR_ - Actionable - Level 2: significant thought and effort required to close out with high impact ("_real" observations_). - _Example: Plumbed chemical showers installed in the 90's has a 15-year life span and needs CAPEX retrofit_ _Obviously the two Actionable examples given are on opposite sides of the spectrum, we just need a way to filter the varying impact/caliber of reports._ To update your SOSPES reports, simply click on the pencil icon... ![Observation Michael Arredondo 520 Notes Attachment...](Files/Exported%20image%2020260127124201-2.png) ...and update the tags. ![Observation Tags Confined Spaces Electrical Enviro...](Files/Exported%20image%2020260127124206-3.png) When all SOSPES reports are retro updated with the new tags, we'll be able to [export](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgo.sospes.com%2FDataExport%3FreportId%3D1&data=05%7C02%7Cdnuckolls%40stackinfra.com%7C03d16b88b2b9432980a008dd5c003b64%7C429094164ba84195a5956ae640290c7d%7C0%7C0%7C638767878257237294%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=N9PPBCi0a%2BqEOJq2QN0JO8tKuDQFXq9G3GiCn2bO3eE%3D&reserved=0) [](https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgo.sospes.com%2FDataExport%3FreportId%3D1&data=05%7C02%7Cdnuckolls%40stackinfra.com%7C03d16b88b2b9432980a008dd5c003b64%7C429094164ba84195a5956ae640290c7d%7C0%7C0%7C638767878257255964%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=y8xHo70BsY45XS5Hf9R30YOJT5UwWhh%2BbP57xY%2FqIsQ%3D&reserved=0)as normal and filter by **ObservationTags**. Here’s a breakdown of Zapier’s key pricing plans as of the latest update (June 2025):
 
**🆓** **Free Plan**

- **Cost:** $0/month
- **Features:**
    - 100 tasks/month
    - Unlimited Zaps (two-step only)
    - Access to AI power-ups (zap creation, mapping, troubleshooting) ([zapier.com](https://zapier.com/pricing?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
- **Best if:** You’re experimenting with basic automations, or using fewer than 100 tasks monthly.
 
**👤** **Professional Plan**

- **Cost:** $19.99/month (billed annually) or ~$29.99/month (monthly)
- **Includes:**
    - Minimum of 750 tasks/month (scales with usage) ([capterra.com](https://www.capterra.com/p/130182/Zapier/pricing/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
    - Multi-step Zaps
    - Webhooks & Filters
    - Unlimited access to premium apps
    - 2-minute polling interval
    - Email support + live chat (if ≥2,000 tasks) ([zapier.com](https://zapier.com/pricing?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [capterra.com](https://www.capterra.com/p/130182/Zapier/pricing/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
- **Best if:** You need more complex automations that go beyond two-step workflows.
 
**👨‍💼** **Team Plan**

- **Cost:** $69/month (billed annually) or ~$103.50/month (monthly)
- **Includes everything in Professional**, plus:
    - Starts at 2,000 tasks/month ([capterra.com](https://www.capterra.com/p/130182/Zapier/pricing/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
    - Multiple users (seat-based)
    - Shared app connections, workspaces, folders
    - SAML SSO (via add-on) and audit logs
    - 1-minute polling interval
    - Premier support ([zapier.com](https://zapier.com/pricing?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [capterra.com](https://www.capterra.com/p/130182/Zapier/pricing/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
- **Best if:** You’re working on automations collaboratively in a small team.
 
**🏢** **Enterprise Plan**

- **Cost:** Custom pricing (contact sales)
- **Includes:**
    - Unlimited users
    - Annual task limits
    - Advanced admin controls, observability tools
    - Technical Account Manager & dedicated support ([zapier.com](https://zapier.com/blog/zapier-plan-improvements-2024/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [zapier.com](https://zapier.com/pricing?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [thedigitalprojectmanager.com](https://thedigitalprojectmanager.com/tools/zapier-pricing/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
- **Best if:** You need enterprise-grade security, oversight, and scale.
 
**💡** **Considerations for Your Setup**  
Since you already have:

- **Notion (personal annual plan)**
- **SOSPES (through work)**

The **Free plan** might not be enough if you're triggering many workflows or need \>100 monthly tasks. On the other hand, the **Professional plan** is a cost-effective step up priced at $19.99/year, and it offers webhooks—which is crucial if SOSPES can send webhook notifications to Zapier. The **Team plan** makes sense only if multiple colleagues will build or manage these automations.  
Also, remember:

- Annual billing gives you a **33% discount** across paid tiers ([capterra.com](https://www.capterra.com/p/130182/Zapier/pricing/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [zapier.com](https://zapier.com/pricing?utm_source=chatgpt.com)).
- You can **scale your task limit** as needed without changing plans.
- Go with **monthly billing** first if you’re unsure—then switch to annual to save once things stabilize.
 
**✅** **Suggested Next Steps**

1. Check the volume of events/tasks you expect from SOSPES—for example, how many alerts or logs you'll be sending into Notion monthly.
2. If it’s modest (\<750), monthly **Professional** is a great fit.
3. Opt for **annual billing** if you’re ready, to lock in a 33% discount.
4. Set up a test **webhook workflow** between SOSPES → Zapier → Notion, tune it, and monitor for task usage.

**Gap Analysis: DIG Underground Utility Protection Plan vs. Holder STACK Utility Avoidance Program (UAP)**  
**Key Focus Areas:**

1. **Excavation Safety**
2. **Utility Avoidance and Protection**
3. **Crane Operations**
 
**Excavation Safety**

|   |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|
|**Criteria**|**Holder STACK UAP**|**DIG Plan**|**Gaps Identified**|
|**Pre-Excavation Planning**|Requires detailed UAP, including risk assessments, permits, and daily checklists before work begins.|Emphasizes pre-excavation planning via 811 calls and site walkthroughs.|DIG lacks detailed permit requirements and checklist formalization for daily operations.|
|**Excavation Tolerance Zone**|6 feet for high-risk utilities; requires hand-digging or potholing within this zone.|24 inches tolerance zone; recommends hand digging and vacuum excavation.|DIG’s tolerance zone is smaller; may conflict with Holder’s higher safety margin.|
|**Potholing/Utility Verification**|Mandatory hydrovac potholing to confirm all utility locations.|Permits vacuum excavation but not explicitly required for all utilities.|DIG lacks a universal potholing mandate for utility verification.|
|**Excavation Safety Protocols**|Requires spotters, barricades, and daily safety checklists.|Spotters and observers are mentioned but less detailed; relies on general safety practices.|DIG provides less structure for spotters and daily checklists.|
 
**Utility Avoidance and Protection**

|   |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|
|**Criteria**|**Holder STACK UAP**|**DIG Plan**|**Gaps Identified**|
|**Utility Marking Standards**|Adheres to APWA color codes and mandates clear marking and tracing of utilities.|Highlights marking preservation and documentation; uses APWA color codes.|DIG does not specify trace wire installation or marking at equivalent detail.|
|**Utility Locate Process**|Requires private and public locates; all must be verified on-site.|811-based system; emphasizes contractor responsibility for locate tickets.|DIG lacks Holder’s formal sign-off and mandatory model integration for locates.|
|**Marking Documentation**|Requires dated photos, sketches, and model updates for utility locations.|Recommends photos and sketches for record-keeping but lacks integration into VDC models.|DIG’s documentation practices are less rigorous.|
 
**Crane Operations**

|   |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|
|**Criteria**|**Holder STACK UAP**|**DIG Plan**|**Gaps Identified**|
|**Crane Safety Near Utilities**|Requires limits of approach, spotters, and daily verification of work zones.|No specific guidelines for crane operations near utilities.|DIG lacks protocols for crane operations and safety measures around overhead utilities.|
|**High-Risk Utility Awareness**|Mandates critical utility review and spotter assignment within 15 feet of live utilities.|Observers mentioned but no explicit protocols for high-risk operations near utilities.|DIG provides no specific high-risk review process for crane work near utilities.|
 
**Recommendations for DIG Plan Alignment**

1. **Permit Processes:**
    - Incorporate detailed permits for excavation activities, similar to Holder's Excavation Permits.
    - Require formal approval and sign-offs, including site-specific risk assessments.
2. **Safety Protocols:**
    - Expand excavation safety protocols to include daily checklists, mandatory spotters, and crane-specific safety measures.
    - Adopt a 6-foot tolerance zone for critical utilities.
3. **Utility Verification:**
    - Make hydrovac potholing mandatory for all utility verifications and incorporate updates into models like VDC/BIM.
4. **Crane Operations:**
    - Develop clear guidelines for crane safety, including proximity to utilities, spotter requirements, and limits of approach.
5. **Documentation Standards:**
    - Enhance documentation requirements to include integration into as-built models and dated photo evidence for all utility locations.
6. **Training and Competency:**
    - Require competent person training for all personnel involved in utility identification and excavation.

**Refined DIG Underground Utility Protection Plan**  
**1. Pre-Excavation Planning**  
**1.1 Mandatory Permit System:**

- Implement an Excavation Permit process requiring the following:
    - As-built drawings.
    - Utility maps and confirmed locates.
    - Hydrovac potholing results.
    - Approval from a competent person and the project manager.
- Include detailed daily checklists for excavation and crane operations.

**1.2 Site-Specific Utility Avoidance Plan:**

- Create and submit a site-specific Utility Avoidance Plan (UAP) integrating:
    - Project risks.
    - Protection measures for high-risk utilities.
    - Excavation zones and access routes.

**1.3 Daily Safety Meetings:**

- Conduct daily pre-task meetings to:
    - Review permits.
    - Confirm utility markings.
    - Assign responsibilities for spotters and equipment operators.
 
**2. Utility Avoidance and Protection**  
**2.1 Utility Locating and Verification:**

- Require both public (811) and private utility locates for all projects.
- Mandate potholing (hydrovac or equivalent) for all utility verification before excavation begins.
- Use trace wires and marking tapes for all temporary and permanent utility installations.

**2.2 Documentation:**

- Maintain dated photo, video, and sketch records of:
    - Utility markings before excavation.
    - Confirmed utility locations after potholing.
- Update as-built drawings and VDC models after each verification.

**2.3 Tolerance Zone Requirements:**

- Enforce a 6-foot tolerance zone for critical utilities.
- Require soft digging or vacuum excavation within this zone.
 
**3. Crane Operations**  
**3.1 Crane-Specific Safety Protocols:**

- Develop and enforce protocols for cranes operating near utilities, including:
    - Limits of approach (minimum 15 feet from live utilities).
    - Spotter assignment for all crane activities near utilities.
    - Verification of work zones and load paths during daily checks.

**3.2 Critical Utility Review:**

- Mandate that work within 15 feet of high-risk utilities undergoes:
    - Risk review by the UAP Champion or competent person.
    - Assignment of a dedicated observer for the operation.
 
**4. Incident Response and Documentation**  
**4.1 Incident Reporting:**

- Establish a formal reporting protocol for:
    - Utility strikes or near misses.
    - Observed mismarked or unmarked utilities.
- Include immediate notification to utility owners, 811, and emergency services where applicable.

**4.2 Post-Incident Analysis:**

- Conduct root cause analysis to identify failures.
- Incorporate lessons learned into updated UAPs.

**4.3 Record Retention:**

- Maintain records for all excavation activities, incidents, and resolutions for at least 5 years.
 
**Implementation Roadmap**  
**Phase 1: Planning and Alignment (Month 1-2)**  
**Action Items:**

- Review current DIG processes against the refined plan.
- Develop templates for Excavation Permits, daily checklists, and incident reports.
- Train staff on new utility locating and documentation standards.

**Milestones:**

- Finalize templates and approval workflows.
- Distribute the updated DIG Underground Utility Protection Plan to all teams.
 
**Phase 2: Training and Rollout (Month 3-4)**  
**Action Items:**

- Conduct training sessions for:
    - Utility verification and potholing techniques.
    - Excavation safety protocols.
    - Crane safety standards near utilities.
- Implement daily pre-task meetings and permit reviews.

**Milestones:**

- 100% of personnel trained and certified on new standards.
- Begin use of updated permits and checklists on all projects.
 
**Phase 3: Monitoring and Feedback (Month 5-6)**  
**Action Items:**

- Assign UAP Champions to oversee compliance on active sites.
- Audit initial projects for adherence to updated protocols.
- Collect feedback from teams to identify gaps or inefficiencies.

**Milestones:**

- Complete audits for at least 3 active projects.
- Adjust plan based on feedback and audit findings.
 
**Phase 4: Full Implementation (Month 7 and Beyond)**  
**Action Items:**

- Enforce penalties for non-compliance.
- Expand record-keeping infrastructure for as-built updates and incident logs.
- Establish a regular review cycle for plan updates.

**Milestones:**

- Achieve zero incidents related to utility strikes or excavation errors.
- Continuous improvement through periodic reviews and retraining.

\\|e: [fnunez@stackinfra.com](mailto:fnunez@stackinfra.com)\\|| || **From:** Matt Honaker \<[mhonaker@stackinfra.com](mailto:mhonaker@stackinfra.com)\> Sent: Wednesday, January 15, 2025 8:41 AM To: Donna Lynch \<[dlynch@stackinfra.com](mailto:dlynch@stackinfra.com)\>; Seann McWilliams \<[smcwilliams@stackinfra.com](mailto:smcwilliams@stackinfra.com)\> Cc: Felicia Nuñez \<[fnunez@stackinfra.com](mailto:fnunez@stackinfra.com)\>; Tom Harris \<[tharris@stackinfra.com](mailto:tharris@stackinfra.com)\>; Jesse Kenser \<[jkenser@stackinfra.com](mailto:jkenser@stackinfra.com)\> Subject: RE: [EXTERNAL] Chubb Risk Engineering Visit Result for Stack Infrastructure   Hi Donna,   Here is my feedback on their recommendations:   **Fire Response Planning for Lithium-Ion Systems** I do not agree with their recommendation regarding our Lithium batteries. Just a guess but they likely did not look into the types of lithium-ion before making this recommendation. Most people see Tesla battery fires, cellphone batteries exploding on airplanes, and various other news about the dangers of them. However, the batteries we have are Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4). With a standard Lithium-Ion battery fire can propagate from one jar to another easily. The same can be said for VRLA batteries during a thermal runaway event. Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries do not have this problem. Narada tested this design in accordance with ANSI/CAN/UL 9540A. Multiple samples were tested, and cells were forced into a thermal runaway event. The fire never propagated to another jar and was contained to the single failure. Those results mean these are safer than VRLAs.   A couple more things to note: - Lithium-Ion batteries do not off gas. VRLAs can off gas during certain conditions and they release hydrogen, which is obviously dangerous. Lithium batteries do not do this. - When these were installed our sprinkler company brought out their engineer to verify we had sufficient fire suppression in place, we do. - NFPA suggests ABC extinguishers because it could be either a class B or C fire. We have all ABCs in the facility. - The city inspected our installation and site for the permit. All firewalls and fire doors are installed according to code and the city’s requirements.   **Water Damage Mitigation Program** Do we really need it? I don’t think so. All our equipment is installed on 4” concrete pads. We would need a ridiculous amount of water to be released for it to become a problem. Additionally, in the areas where it really matters, we have the pre-action fire system. Accidental release in those areas would be unlikely. The only release that could impact us would be if a 10” chilled water pipe burst. The pressure is so low that it wouldn’t be an instant flood but all the water in the pipe could be released if the hole was big enough. In that scenario, our equipment being up on 4” pads would protect us.   **Inspection of the Lightning Arrestor System** I agree we should be inspecting this, and as Tom pointed out, it is called for in the maintenance standard. This has been something we have discussed with TJ and Spencer many times and a real solution/decision has never been made. The problem is we don’t have a safe way to do it. We inspect the system on the main roof, that’s not a problem. The chilled water storage towers, which are the highest point, are where the issue comes in. We don’t have a safe way to get up there. Our 2-man lift is not high enough and according to David N the ladders that are installed on the towers can’t be used. Since we would never need a reason to get up there besides this inspection it got put on the back burner. I am open to any suggestions though.   Thank you,   | | |---| |\| \|
