\\|e: [fnunez@stackinfra.com](mailto:fnunez@stackinfra.com)\\|| || **From:** Matt Honaker \<[mhonaker@stackinfra.com](mailto:mhonaker@stackinfra.com)\> Sent: Wednesday, January 15, 2025 8:41 AM To: Donna Lynch \<[dlynch@stackinfra.com](mailto:dlynch@stackinfra.com)\>; Seann McWilliams \<[smcwilliams@stackinfra.com](mailto:smcwilliams@stackinfra.com)\> Cc: Felicia Nuñez \<[fnunez@stackinfra.com](mailto:fnunez@stackinfra.com)\>; Tom Harris \<[tharris@stackinfra.com](mailto:tharris@stackinfra.com)\>; Jesse Kenser \<[jkenser@stackinfra.com](mailto:jkenser@stackinfra.com)\> Subject: RE: [EXTERNAL] Chubb Risk Engineering Visit Result for Stack Infrastructure   Hi Donna,   Here is my feedback on their recommendations:   **Fire Response Planning for Lithium-Ion Systems** I do not agree with their recommendation regarding our Lithium batteries. Just a guess but they likely did not look into the types of lithium-ion before making this recommendation. Most people see Tesla battery fires, cellphone batteries exploding on airplanes, and various other news about the dangers of them. However, the batteries we have are Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4). With a standard Lithium-Ion battery fire can propagate from one jar to another easily. The same can be said for VRLA batteries during a thermal runaway event. Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries do not have this problem. Narada tested this design in accordance with ANSI/CAN/UL 9540A. Multiple samples were tested, and cells were forced into a thermal runaway event. The fire never propagated to another jar and was contained to the single failure. Those results mean these are safer than VRLAs.   A couple more things to note: - Lithium-Ion batteries do not off gas. VRLAs can off gas during certain conditions and they release hydrogen, which is obviously dangerous. Lithium batteries do not do this. - When these were installed our sprinkler company brought out their engineer to verify we had sufficient fire suppression in place, we do. - NFPA suggests ABC extinguishers because it could be either a class B or C fire. We have all ABCs in the facility. - The city inspected our installation and site for the permit. All firewalls and fire doors are installed according to code and the city’s requirements.   **Water Damage Mitigation Program** Do we really need it? I don’t think so. All our equipment is installed on 4” concrete pads. We would need a ridiculous amount of water to be released for it to become a problem. Additionally, in the areas where it really matters, we have the pre-action fire system. Accidental release in those areas would be unlikely. The only release that could impact us would be if a 10” chilled water pipe burst. The pressure is so low that it wouldn’t be an instant flood but all the water in the pipe could be released if the hole was big enough. In that scenario, our equipment being up on 4” pads would protect us.   **Inspection of the Lightning Arrestor System** I agree we should be inspecting this, and as Tom pointed out, it is called for in the maintenance standard. This has been something we have discussed with TJ and Spencer many times and a real solution/decision has never been made. The problem is we don’t have a safe way to do it. We inspect the system on the main roof, that’s not a problem. The chilled water storage towers, which are the highest point, are where the issue comes in. We don’t have a safe way to get up there. Our 2-man lift is not high enough and according to David N the ladders that are installed on the towers can’t be used. Since we would never need a reason to get up there besides this inspection it got put on the back burner. I am open to any suggestions though.   Thank you,   | | |---| |\| \|

**2024.11.20 NON-Permit Required Confined Space Evaluation (NVA02D)**

- Verify there is an entrant, attendant, and job supervisor.
- Team Fishel to provide proof of training on Confined Space Entry for the entrant, attendant, and job supervisor for this scope of work.
- Verify the atmospheric monitoring device has been recently calibrated per manufacturer's specifications.
- Verify crew has a means of testing the atmosphere in the space via a hose or wand attachment to the atmospheric monitoring device.
- Verify atmospheric readings will be checked and made safe and logged periodically or continuously on the Confined Space Permit.
    
    - Will Team Fishel be logging periodic atmospheric monitoring results on the "Example A: Confined Space Pre-entry Checklist & Inspection Form"?
    - ![A document with text and numbers Description autom...](Files/Exported%20image%2020260127104522-0.png)
- Verify a barricade around the entry point of the confined space has been erected.
- Verify local foot traffic cannot enter the work area (ex: additional barricade, signs, etc.).
- Verify an air mover will be used to continuously push fresh air into the confined space.
- **Verify a tripod is present and ready to use in the event of the confined space meeting the criteria of a permit-required confined space. **

Thank you, Can you please provide a bullet pointed list of exactly which Environmental, Health, and Safety trainings are required to be given by employers to managers or supervisors in Ontario, Canada?
   

In Ontario, Canada, employers are legally required to provide specific Environmental, Health, and Safety (EHS) training to managers and supervisors. The mandatory training includes:

- **Basic Occupational Health and Safety Awareness Training:** Supervisors must complete this program within one week of assuming their duties. The training covers:
    - Duties and rights of workers under the Occupational Health and Safety Act (OHSA).
    - Duties of employers and supervisors under the OHSA.
    - Roles of health and safety representatives and Joint Health and Safety Committees (JHSCs).
    - Procedures for recognizing, assessing, and controlling workplace hazards.
    - Sources of information on occupational health and safety. citeturn0search1
- **Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) Training:** Supervisors overseeing workers who handle or are exposed to hazardous materials must receive WHMIS training to understand safe handling, storage, and emergency procedures related to these substances. citeturn0search3
- **Workplace Violence and Harassment Training:** Employers are required to develop and implement policies addressing workplace violence and harassment. Supervisors must be trained on these policies to effectively prevent and respond to incidents. citeturn0search3
- **Sector-Specific Training:** Depending on the industry, additional training may be mandatory. For example:
    - **Working at Heights Training:** Required for supervisors in the construction sector who oversee workers performing tasks at heights.
    - **Confined Space Entry Training:** Necessary for supervisors managing work in confined spaces across various industries. citeturn0search6

Employers must maintain records of all completed training to demonstrate compliance with Ontario's occupational health and safety regulations.

## The error message "Query Parameters - Parameter 1 - There weren't enough elements in the enumeration to complete the operation." in Power BI typically occurs when Power Query encounters an issue with a parameter or data source, often related to:
 
1. **Incorrect or Missing Values in Parameters**: The parameter might not have a valid value or is not set properly.
2. **Data Source Issues**: The query depends on a data source that does not provide enough data or returns fewer rows/columns than expected.
3. **Logic Mismatch in Queries**: The query logic might be referencing elements that are not present in the data, such as columns, rows, or tables that do not exist.

Here’s how to troubleshoot this issue:
 
**1. Check Parameter Value**

- Open the **Manage Parameters** pane in Power Query Editor.
- Verify that Parameter 1 (or the specific parameter mentioned in the error) is correctly configured and has a valid value.
    - If the parameter is dynamic, ensure its source data is valid and returns results.
 
**2. Validate Query Dependencies**

- Inspect the query that uses Parameter 1.
- Look for:
    - Missing or null values.
    - Hardcoded references to columns or tables that no longer exist in the data source.
- Test the parameter manually in the query editor to ensure it returns the expected results.
 
**3. Examine Data Source**

- Check the underlying data source to ensure it provides the expected data.
    - Ensure the data source connection is valid and that it returns rows and columns as expected.
    - If the data source has been updated or changed, verify the query is aligned with the new schema.
 
**4. Error in Data Transformation Steps**

- Review all transformation steps in the affected query:
    - Look for errors or warnings in intermediate steps.
    - Confirm that each step returns valid data (e.g., by previewing the data).
- Use **View Native Query** to ensure the SQL query (if applicable) is valid.
 
**5. Update or Reset the Parameter**

- If the parameter is set dynamically (e.g., based on a list of values from a data source):
    - Refresh the data source or recreate the parameter.
- If it’s manually set, ensure it’s within the expected range of values.
 
**6. Recreate the Parameter**

- If troubleshooting does not resolve the issue:
    - Delete Parameter 1.
    - Recreate it and reassign it in the query.
 
**Additional Tips:**

- Use the **Query Diagnostics** feature in Power BI to analyze how the query processes the parameter and identify the root cause.
- Check for issues related to regional or data format differences (e.g., number/date formats).

If you continue to face the error, providing more context, such as details about Parameter 1, its expected usage, and the query logic, can help diagnose the problem further.

- Verify there is an entrant, attendant, and job supervisor.

- Verify the atmospheric monitoring device has been recently calibrated per manufacturer's specifications.

- Verify atmospheric readings will be checked and made safe and logged periodically or continuously on the Confined Space Permit.
